ANALYSIS

[9] The Appellant benefits from an initial presumption that his sworn statements are true unless there are valid reasons to doubt them. As the Appellant has argued, this initial presumption extends to the evidence that the Appellant has adduced as credible documentation.
Attempts to return to Pakistan undermine credibility of subjective fear

[10] The Appellant has alleged that he had a secret same-sex relationship with his former partner Z. for over 10 years from the year 2000-2011.2 The Appellant has alleged that a local religious scholar somehow discovered that the two were in a secret relationship. The religious scholar allegedly gathered a group of men and assaulted and threatened the Appellant and Z. before letting them go. The Appellant vaguely wrote in his narrative that his extended family found out about the incident shortly thereafter "from the people of the area."3 The Appellant allegedly received threats of death from various people including his own family members. The Appellant then left for the USA and Z. left for the United Kingdom. His parents allegedly had to pack up and move to another city, Lahore, to escape the humiliation.

[11] The Appellant has written that it is "internationally known and recognized" that Pakistan is extremely conservative and that the situation for gay men is "draconian."4 He has written that "it is known to all and sundry that religious extremism is presently at its peak in Pakistan" and that "there seems no end to this wave of religious extremism in Pakistan in the near and foreseeable future."5 The Appellant has noted that several gay men have been killed in the past in Pakistan.

[12] It is in this alleged personal and country context that the Appellant stated that he attempted on two separate occasions to return to Pakistan, even going so far as to book airline tickets. He was motivated to return, he testified, because his aging parents "currently live by themselves in Lahore" and they "need someone to care for them."6 He wrote in his narrative that during the time of his attempted returns "I had not completely made up my mind about living permanently in the USA or any other Western country, due to my parents' plight..." He also testified that the only reason he did not return was because his parents stopped him.

[13] At this point, the RPD reminded the Appellant that according to his Basis of Claim family list, he has a sister currently residing in Lahore approximately 1km from their parents' house.7 The RPD asked several questions about the sister's role, and the Appellant eventually conceded that his sister was able to take care of the parents. The RPD found that the allegations regarding the Appellant's hesitation to settle in the West and his desire to return to Pakistan to take care of his isolated parents was misleading and false. Further, the RPD found that the Appellant's allegations of subjective fear were undermined by his attempts to return to a situation he allegedly knew was highly persecutory.

[14] The Appellant has argued on appeal that these findings are microscopic and impose an unduly onerous requirement on the Appellant. The Appellant has submitted that the fact that he wanted to return despite his sister being there does not detract from his credibility. The Appellant has argued that the RPD speculated as to what his mindset was during that period.

[15] In my independent review, I agree with the RPD that this testimony undermines the Appellant's allegations of subjective fear. By explaining that he was unsettled in the West because of his parents' "plight" of isolation, the Appellant attempted to explain his delay and eventual failure to claim asylum in the USA (I analyze the actual failure to claim more closely in another section below). This, in my opinion, brings the allegation of his desire to return to Pakistan from the periphery to the core of the claim because it touches directly on the Appellant's subjective fear of the allegedly serious persecution he had suffered and would suffer in the future as a gay man in Pakistan. The Appellant's premise, that he was motivated to return to Pakistan despite intense risk because of his parents' plight and because they needed someone to take care of them, is seriously undermined by the fact that emerged only later, that his sister not only lives close by the parents but that she takes care of them, too. I do not see this as speculative, since the RPD relied on the Appellant's own testimony and evidence at different points to come to its finding. I do not see this as microscopic since it deals with the Appellant's own explanation for his delay and failure to claim asylum in the USA and is therefore central to his subjective fear.

[16] For all the reasons above, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's several attempts to return to Pakistan undermine the credibility of his allegations of subjective fear.

[17] The Appellant wrote in his narrative that he had entered the USA on numerous occasions during his secret relationship with Z. The Appellant had been in the USA on a student visa to attend XXXX XXXX XXXX school during that time and had travelled back and forth between his temporary residence in the USA and his permanent home in Pakistan. The Appellant entered the USA for the last time in 2011, at which point he alleges he fled from Pakistan after his relationship and sexual orientation were discovered by his family and the wider community.

[24] In my independent review, I agree with the RPD that the various irregularities in the receipt undermine its credibility and the credibility of the allegation that the Appellant ever sought legal advice to regularize his status in the USA. I find it extremely unusual that a receipt of a professional lawyer in the USA would contain absolutely no identifiable information. There is no evidence to suggest that this is normal practice of lawyers in the Pakistani community or anywhere else, and no evidence to support the speculation that perhaps the lawyer was planning to evade his taxes. Even more unusual, though, is the apparent two-year gap that the RPD pointed out in the date of the receipt compared with the date the Appellant stated that he was seeking legal advice. The Appellant has never explained this discrepancy. The Appellant has not explained why his memory is so blank when it comes to any details whatsoever regarding his interactions with lawyers in the USA. If the Appellant could not remember the names or locations of the lawyers' offices at the hearing, and especially because the RPD raised the issue in its decision, I would have expected the Appellant to make serious efforts to try to piece this information together for his appeal. It is common knowledge that lawyers in the USA are professionals and are publicly regulated by bar associations. I have absolutely no evidence that the Appellant has made any attempt to track down any of the lawyers he allegedly spoke with, despite their publicly registered status. I agree with the RPD that this receipt is likely fraudulent and that the Appellant is not credible regarding his allegations that he ever sought legal advice to regularize his status in the USA.

[37] The Appellant's third explanation, that he was concerned for his parents who were alone in Lahore with nobody to care for them and attempted to return twice to a highly persecutory situation to do so was also found not to be credible, and again I will not restate my reasons for this. [38] The Appellant's fourth explanation, that he did not apply for asylum in the USA because he was concerned that his claim would not be accepted and because of the ongoing discrimination against Muslim people in the USA is not sufficient in my opinion. While I accept that ongoing anti-Muslim discrimination in the USA is an objective concern, the Appellant made no mention of having this concern personally in his detailed narrative and explanations for his failure to claim. The explanation only arose at the RPD hearing. The facts of this case show that the Appellant was living, going to school, and working in the USA for a total of 12 years (from 2006 to 2018). The Appellant was not, so to speak, living under the radar in the USA during this time. He has alleged that apart from living, going to school, and working in the USA, he was actively socializing with other gay men and attending bars and nightclubs. I would expect that if anti-Muslim sentiment in the USA or fear of rejection were a significant factor in the Appellant's mind, the Appellant would have attempted to regularize his status elsewhere. I would also expect the Appellant to have at least articulated this reason in his narrative instead of including allegations about how active he was in USA society and how he planned to apply for status on the basis of his educational and work integration.

[40] The RPD noted that the Appellant alleged that he had been an active member of the gay community in the USA for at least five years, and that he had alleged that he was an active member of the Canadian gay community for approximately two years at the time of the RPD hearing. The Appellant wrote and testified that in this period, he had been going to bars and nightclubs, meeting numerous other gay people, and had engaged in numerous interpersonal relationships with other gay men, including sexual relationships. However, the Appellant testified that none of these relationships were long-lasting. The RPD noted that, before these relationships, the Appellant had alleged that he had an 11-year romantic relationship with Z., numerous years of which the relationship was maintained over long distance between the USA and Pakistan.

[41] The RPD noted that the Appellant had provided no corroborative evidence, such as photos or letters, from any other person with whom he had a personal connection in the gay community. The RPD noted that the Appellant had attended the 519 Community Centre in Toronto on a weekly basis from XXXX 2018 to XXXX 2020, and that he had allegedly been open about his orientation while there. The RPD found the lack of evidence from individuals in the gay community problematic, given the Appellant's specific allegations.

[42] The Appellant explained that he was too fearful to get evidence of his connections to other gay people but did not elaborate. He explained that he had never thought of getting a letter from anyone he met in Canada that had personal knowledge of his orientation.

[43] The RPD found that the lack of evidence was unreasonable for a bright, sophisticated XXXX graduate of the Appellant's profile. The RPD found that given the understandable lack of evidence from Pakistan, the Appellant would have been expected to have produced some sort of corroborative evidence of his allegedly extensive integration into the gay communities in the USA and Canada. The RPD noted that there are some instances in which it is not reasonable to expect evidence will be available, but no reason was given regarding why the Appellant could produce no evidence of his allegedly extensive public socializing in the USA.

[44] On appeal, the Appellant has argued that his relationship with Z. was secretive, and they lost contact after 2011, so it is unduly onerous to expect any evidence of that relationship. He has further argued that the expectation of evidence from the USA or Canada is unreasonable because he holds reasonable ongoing fears and reservations about his orientation, notwithstanding the fact that he has had numerous interpersonal relationships and has gone to bars and nightclubs in the USA. The Appellant has argued that the statement of attendance from the 519 Community Centre is corroborative evidence of his orientation and that the RPD ignored this. In any event, the Appellant argues, the lack of evidence finding is not based on inconsistencies and a lack of evidence is not sufficient on its own to rebut his presumption of truthfulness.

[45] In my independent assessment, I do consider it quite unusual that the Appellant in his personal circumstances is entirely unable to provide corroborative evidence from even one single personal connection. The Appellant was allegedly in a long-distance relationship for over 10 years, and though I understand that the relationship was secretive, the Appellant has made reference to both telephone communication and social media activity with Z. I find it quite unusual that the Appellant would be able to point to no "digital fingerprint" of the Appellant's past communications with Z. I find it more unusual that the Appellant is unable to provide evidence from any of his past personal connections in the gay communities in the USA and Canada. I do not accept the Appellant's explanation that he holds ongoing fears and reservations about his orientation in the USA and Canada. In my opinion, the Appellant's alleged public activities in which he has stated that he voluntarily attended numerous bars and nightclubs and had numerous personal relationships with people outweighs the fear of his orientation that I can accept he may hold. Even more unusual, in my opinion, is the fact that the Appellant has shown no particular interest in gathering this evidence. I have no evidence showing that the Appellant has attempted to find or reach out to any of his current or past connections in the gay community with whom he has ever socialized. Furthermore, I have no evidence showing that the Appellant has attempted to contact any of the bars or nightclubs the Appellant allegedly used to frequent in order to gather evidence of his past attendance or connections.

[46] I am mindful of the basic legal premise that there is no fundamental requirement for corroborative evidence. For this reason, I find that the lack of corroborative evidence of any personal connections to people in the gay community does not warrant its own negative credibility inference. However, this lack of corroborative evidence does mean that the claim must instead be decided on the remaining evidence that the Appellant has provided.
Letter from the 519 Community Centre

[47] The RPD did not directly address the letter from the 519 Community Centre (a well-known institutional hub for the gay community in Toronto). This was an error. The letter from the 519 states that the Appellant has attended a newcomer orientation session and that he has attended 13 weeks of an integration support group aimed at the 2SLGBT+ community. I consider this letter credible in confirming that the Appellant has, since he applied for refugee status in Canada, attended these sessions. The letter gives no indication that its author has any specific knowledge of the Appellant's other allegations or of his sexual orientation. However, I accept that the letter is supportive of the Appellant's allegations and it should be weighed against the credibility problems in the final credibility assessment.

[48] The RPD found that the letter from the Appellant's father was not credible, because the letter from the father omitted the allegation that the parents had to flee their hometown for Lahore as a result of the discovery of the Appellant's orientation in 2011. The RPD found that it was not credible that the father would omit this or forget this in his letter because it would have been traumatizing.

[49] On appeal, the Appellant has argued that this document is in fact an affidavit, not a letter. The Appellant argues that it is erroneous to judge it on what it does not say and that the letter is otherwise consistent with the Appellant's narrative.

[50] In my independent review, I do note that the letter contains some minor irregularities. First, the letter is not an affidavit as the Appellant has asserted. It is not sworn or notarized. It appears to me to simply be a letter that was typed, for a reason not explained, on Pakistani affidavit stamp paper. The letter itself uses several specific turns of phrase that are identical to those used in the Appellant's memorandum, which I find unusual since the two documents were allegedly written by different people. I take no negative inferences from these minor irregularities. The Federal Court has been clear that letters should be weighed for what they do say and not what they do not say. I find the RPD's approach to the letter to be erroneous and I take no negative credibility inference. I weigh the letter against the other evidence and the credibility problems above in my conclusion on credibility.

[42] The Appellant explained that he was too fearful to get evidence of his connections to other gay people but did not elaborate. He explained that he had never thought of getting a letter from anyone he met in Canada that had personal knowledge of his orientation.

[43] The RPD found that the lack of evidence was unreasonable for a bright, sophisticated XXXX graduate of the Appellant's profile. The RPD found that given the understandable lack of evidence from Pakistan, the Appellant would have been expected to have produced some sort of corroborative evidence of his allegedly extensive integration into the gay communities in the USA and Canada. The RPD noted that there are some instances in which it is not reasonable to expect evidence will be available, but no reason was given regarding why the Appellant could produce no evidence of his allegedly extensive public socializing in the USA.

[44] On appeal, the Appellant has argued that his relationship with Z. was secretive, and they lost contact after 2011, so it is unduly onerous to expect any evidence of that relationship. He has further argued that the expectation of evidence from the USA or Canada is unreasonable because he holds reasonable ongoing fears and reservations about his orientation, notwithstanding the fact that he has had numerous interpersonal relationships and has gone to bars and nightclubs in the USA. The Appellant has argued that the statement of attendance from the 519 Community Centre is corroborative evidence of his orientation and that the RPD ignored this. In any event, the Appellant argues, the lack of evidence finding is not based on inconsistencies and a lack of evidence is not sufficient on its own to rebut his presumption of truthfulness.

[45] In my independent assessment, I do consider it quite unusual that the Appellant in his personal circumstances is entirely unable to provide corroborative evidence from even one single personal connection. The Appellant was allegedly in a long-distance relationship for over 10 years, and though I understand that the relationship was secretive, the Appellant has made reference to both telephone communication and social media activity with Z. I find it quite unusual that the Appellant would be able to point to no "digital fingerprint" of the Appellant's past communications with Z. I find it more unusual that the Appellant is unable to provide evidence from any of his past personal connections in the gay communities in the USA and Canada. I do not accept the Appellant's explanation that he holds ongoing fears and reservations about his orientation in the USA and Canada. In my opinion, the Appellant's alleged public activities in which he has stated that he voluntarily attended numerous bars and nightclubs and had numerous personal relationships with people outweighs the fear of his orientation that I can accept he may hold. Even more unusual, in my opinion, is the fact that the Appellant has shown no particular interest in gathering this evidence. I have no evidence showing that the Appellant has attempted to find or reach out to any of his current or past connections in the gay community with whom he has ever socialized. Furthermore, I have no evidence showing that the Appellant has attempted to contact any of the bars or nightclubs the Appellant allegedly used to frequent in order to gather evidence of his past attendance or connections.

[46] I am mindful of the basic legal premise that there is no fundamental requirement for corroborative evidence. For this reason, I find that the lack of corroborative evidence of any personal connections to people in the gay community does not warrant its own negative credibility inference. However, this lack of corroborative evidence does mean that the claim must instead be decided on the remaining evidence that the Appellant has provided.
Letter from the 519 Community Centre

[47] The RPD did not directly address the letter from the 519 Community Centre (a well-known institutional hub for the gay community in Toronto). This was an error. The letter from the 519 states that the Appellant has attended a newcomer orientation session and that he has attended 13 weeks of an integration support group aimed at the 2SLGBT+ community. I consider this letter credible in confirming that the Appellant has, since he applied for refugee status in Canada, attended these sessions. The letter gives no indication that its author has any specific knowledge of the Appellant's other allegations or of his sexual orientation. However, I accept that the letter is supportive of the Appellant's allegations and it should be weighed against the credibility problems in the final credibility assessment.
Letter from the Appellant's father

[48] The RPD found that the letter from the Appellant's father was not credible, because the letter from the father omitted the allegation that the parents had to flee their hometown for Lahore as a result of the discovery of the Appellant's orientation in 2011. The RPD found that it was not credible that the father would omit this or forget this in his letter because it would have been traumatizing.

[49] On appeal, the Appellant has argued that this document is in fact an affidavit, not a letter. The Appellant argues that it is erroneous to judge it on what it does not say and that the letter is otherwise consistent with the Appellant's narrative.

[50] In my independent review, I do note that the letter contains some minor irregularities. First, the letter is not an affidavit as the Appellant has asserted. It is not sworn or notarized. It appears to me to simply be a letter that was typed, for a reason not explained, on Pakistani affidavit stamp paper. The letter itself uses several specific turns of phrase that are identical to those used in the Appellant's memorandum, which I find unusual since the two documents were allegedly written by different people. I take no negative inferences from these minor irregularities. The Federal Court has been clear that letters should be weighed for what they do say and not what they do not say. I find the RPD's approach to the letter to be erroneous and I take no negative credibility inference. I weigh the letter against the other evidence and the credibility problems above in my conclusion on credibility.

Conclusion on credibility: the Appellant's presumption of truthfulness is rebutted

[61] When I consider all the evidence as a whole, I find that I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted. I find this way because the Appellant has not reasonably explained various problems covering numerous areas of his core allegations of subjective fear, including his attempts to return to Pakistan, inconsistencies in his evidence related to his interactions with refugee lawyers, and his long-standing failure to claim status in the USA. The Appellant provided some corroborative documents, which I have considered, but I find that they collectively do not overcome or outweigh the credibility problems. I accept that the Appellant has attended a 2SLGBT+ meeting group since he initiated his refugee claim in Canada, but I find this insufficient to reliably establish his core allegation that he is a gay man given the other problems on the record. The Appellant showed no effort to gather other corroborative evidence of his past alleged personal relationships with other gay men, which may very well have overcome the credibility problems had it been reliably adduced. Due to the inconsistencies and other problems in the record, I find the Appellant's testimony and evidence unreliable on the core allegation that he is a gay man, that he has ever been suspected of being a gay man, that he has been persecuted in the past, and that he would face a serious possibility of persecution in the future. This finding is determinative of this appeal.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION AND DECISION

[1] The following reasons explain why I am dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant). The Appellant has appealed the Refugee Protection Division's (RPD) February 17, 2021 decision that rejected his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant has asked that I substitute the RPD's decision with my own finding that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, or that I return the file to the RPD for redetermination. I find that the RPD was correct to determine that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee and that he is not a person in need of protection.
BACKGROUND

[2] The Appellant has made the following key allegations in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form and at the RPD hearing:
* That he is a citizen of Pakistan and no other country.
* That he identifies as a gay man. That he has had one significant romantic same-sex relationship spanning several years with a man in Pakistan and he has also been active in the gay community in both the United States of America (USA) and Canada.
* That his family and the Pakistani community in his hometown discovered his orientation. That he was assaulted and threatened in Pakistan.
* That he lived for several years in the USA and then crossed to Canada, where he made his refugee claim.

[3] The RPD found that the Appellant's claim failed because of several credibility issues, including an implausibility finding, an unreasonable omission of evidence, inconsistencies in his letters of support, and unreliable documents.

[4] The Appellant has argued on appeal that the RPD erred by making findings that are speculative, by applying an unduly onerous expectation of corroborative evidence, by ignoring evidence, and by unreasonably weighing and dismissing evidence.
PRELIMINARY MATTERS
No new evidence and no oral hearing

[5] The Appellant has not requested the admission of any new evidence with respect to this appeal and has not sought an oral hearing at the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). As no new evidence was admitted in this appeal, no oral hearing is permitted pursuant to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) s. 110(6).1
The role of the RAD

[6] I have reviewed the entirety of the written record and have listened to the audio recording of the RPD hearing. The RPD had no meaningful advantage over me in assessing the credibility of oral testimony. I have therefore undertaken a review of the correctness of the RPD decision throughout.
Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression

[7] This claim directly involves allegations of persecution related to the Appellant's sexual orientation. As such, I have considered the issues and findings in this appeal through the lens of Guideline 9. I have discussed the impact of the Guideline on my findings in each section in the analysis below.
Credibility as the determinative issue

[8] As I will explain below, I find that the RPD was correct to determine that the Appellant lacks credibility with respect to his allegations of past persecution and of his future risk. This issue is determinative of this appeal.
ANALYSIS

[9] The Appellant benefits from an initial presumption that his sworn statements are true unless there are valid reasons to doubt them. As the Appellant has argued, this initial presumption extends to the evidence that the Appellant has adduced as credible documentation.
Attempts to return to Pakistan undermine credibility of subjective fear

[10] The Appellant has alleged that he had a secret same-sex relationship with his former partner Z. for over 10 years from the year 2000-2011.2 The Appellant has alleged that a local religious scholar somehow discovered that the two were in a secret relationship. The religious scholar allegedly gathered a group of men and assaulted and threatened the Appellant and Z. before letting them go. The Appellant vaguely wrote in his narrative that his extended family found out about the incident shortly thereafter "from the people of the area."3 The Appellant allegedly received threats of death from various people including his own family members. The Appellant then left for the USA and Z. left for the United Kingdom. His parents allegedly had to pack up and move to another city, Lahore, to escape the humiliation.

[11] The Appellant has written that it is "internationally known and recognized" that Pakistan is extremely conservative and that the situation for gay men is "draconian."4 He has written that "it is known to all and sundry that religious extremism is presently at its peak in Pakistan" and that "there seems no end to this wave of religious extremism in Pakistan in the near and foreseeable future."5 The Appellant has noted that several gay men have been killed in the past in Pakistan.

[12] It is in this alleged personal and country context that the Appellant stated that he attempted on two separate occasions to return to Pakistan, even going so far as to book airline tickets. He was motivated to return, he testified, because his aging parents "currently live by themselves in Lahore" and they "need someone to care for them."6 He wrote in his narrative that during the time of his attempted returns "I had not completely made up my mind about living permanently in the USA or any other Western country, due to my parents' plight..." He also testified that the only reason he did not return was because his parents stopped him.

[13] At this point, the RPD reminded the Appellant that according to his Basis of Claim family list, he has a sister currently residing in Lahore approximately 1km from their parents' house.7 The RPD asked several questions about the sister's role, and the Appellant eventually conceded that his sister was able to take care of the parents. The RPD found that the allegations regarding the Appellant's hesitation to settle in the West and his desire to return to Pakistan to take care of his isolated parents was misleading and false. Further, the RPD found that the Appellant's allegations of subjective fear were undermined by his attempts to return to a situation he allegedly knew was highly persecutory.

[14] The Appellant has argued on appeal that these findings are microscopic and impose an unduly onerous requirement on the Appellant. The Appellant has submitted that the fact that he wanted to return despite his sister being there does not detract from his credibility. The Appellant has argued that the RPD speculated as to what his mindset was during that period.

[15] In my independent review, I agree with the RPD that this testimony undermines the Appellant's allegations of subjective fear. By explaining that he was unsettled in the West because of his parents' "plight" of isolation, the Appellant attempted to explain his delay and eventual failure to claim asylum in the USA (I analyze the actual failure to claim more closely in another section below). This, in my opinion, brings the allegation of his desire to return to Pakistan from the periphery to the core of the claim because it touches directly on the Appellant's subjective fear of the allegedly serious persecution he had suffered and would suffer in the future as a gay man in Pakistan. The Appellant's premise, that he was motivated to return to Pakistan despite intense risk because of his parents' plight and because they needed someone to take care of them, is seriously undermined by the fact that emerged only later, that his sister not only lives close by the parents but that she takes care of them, too. I do not see this as speculative, since the RPD relied on the Appellant's own testimony and evidence at different points to come to its finding. I do not see this as microscopic since it deals with the Appellant's own explanation for his delay and failure to claim asylum in the USA and is therefore central to his subjective fear.

[16] For all the reasons above, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's several attempts to return to Pakistan undermine the credibility of his allegations of subjective fear.
The receipt from a lawyer undermines the Appellant's credibility

[17] The Appellant wrote in his narrative that he had entered the USA on numerous occasions during his secret relationship with Z. The Appellant had been in the USA on a student visa to attend XXXX XXXX XXXX school during that time and had travelled back and forth between his temporary residence in the USA and his permanent home in Pakistan. The Appellant entered the USA for the last time in 2011, at which point he alleges he fled from Pakistan after his relationship and sexual orientation were discovered by his family and the wider community.

[18] The Appellant wrote in his narrative that he did not seek asylum in the USA in 2011 because he wanted to complete his studies and then apply for permanent residence after based on his USA education and work experience.8 The Appellant completed his XXXX education in 2012, and subsequently enrolled in a XXXX XXXX XXXX in the USA. In 2013, the Appellant's status at his XXXX was terminated. At that point, the Appellant wrote, he "contacted a few attorneys in the USA to seek their guidance as to how I could obtain legal status in the USA."9 In support of this allegation, the Appellant adduced a receipt that he stated was from one of the lawyers with whom he consulted.10

[19] The RPD noted numerous irregularities with this document. First, the RPD noted that the receipt has no letterhead and no name, location, or any other identifying information regarding who the lawyer was in the transaction. The RPD noted that the receipt was simply handwritten onto a page from a generic receipt booklet. The handwritten receipt simply states that the Appellant paid $150 in cash for a "consultation" and includes only an illegible signature. The receipt is dated XXXX XXXX, 2015, which would place the transaction approximately two years later than the Appellant described his interactions with the lawyers in his narrative.

[20] The RPD asked the Appellant about his interactions with the lawyers and about the irregularities with the receipt. The Appellant explained that he had no memory of any of the lawyers from whom he sought advice, and he simply went into an unknown office and asked someone about legal advice. The Appellant explained that he had never taken a close look at the receipt before. The Appellant did not remember the location of any of the lawyers or their offices.

[21] The Appellant's counsel argued in submissions that this is a customary practice in Pakistan and that lawyers are so busy that it is common to simply write receipts from a blank receipt book. The Appellant's counsel further suggested that the lawyer may have avoided any identifiers on the receipt because they were planning to avoid paying income taxes.

[22] The RPD found that the irregularities in the receipt were not sufficiently explained. The RPD found that the receipt was likely fraudulent and that the Appellant had not sought legal advice on asylum or other routes to legal status in the USA as he had alleged.

[23] On appeal, the Appellant has argued that the lack of specificity in the receipt should not detract from its credibility. In any case, the Appellant argues, the receipt is not related to core aspects of his claim, including his allegations regarding his sexual orientation.

[24] In my independent review, I agree with the RPD that the various irregularities in the receipt undermine its credibility and the credibility of the allegation that the Appellant ever sought legal advice to regularize his status in the USA. I find it extremely unusual that a receipt of a professional lawyer in the USA would contain absolutely no identifiable information. There is no evidence to suggest that this is normal practice of lawyers in the Pakistani community or anywhere else, and no evidence to support the speculation that perhaps the lawyer was planning to evade his taxes. Even more unusual, though, is the apparent two-year gap that the RPD pointed out in the date of the receipt compared with the date the Appellant stated that he was seeking legal advice. The Appellant has never explained this discrepancy. The Appellant has not explained why his memory is so blank when it comes to any details whatsoever regarding his interactions with lawyers in the USA. If the Appellant could not remember the names or locations of the lawyers' offices at the hearing, and especially because the RPD raised the issue in its decision, I would have expected the Appellant to make serious efforts to try to piece this information together for his appeal. It is common knowledge that lawyers in the USA are professionals and are publicly regulated by bar associations. I have absolutely no evidence that the Appellant has made any attempt to track down any of the lawyers he allegedly spoke with, despite their publicly registered status. I agree with the RPD that this receipt is likely fraudulent and that the Appellant is not credible regarding his allegations that he ever sought legal advice to regularize his status in the USA.

[25] The Appellant is correct that this finding does not intersect directly with his allegations regarding his sexual orientation, but it is nevertheless central to his allegations of subjective fear and his explanation for his failure to claim status in the USA. While not determinative on its own, this finding does lead me to a negative credibility inference.
Failure to claim asylum in the USA undermines the Appellant's credibility

[26] The Appellant wrote that he knew he was gay since he was 13 or 14 years old, around the year 1996.11 He wrote that he was in a secret romantic relationship with another man in Pakistan from approximately 2000 to 2011. The Appellant wrote that during this time he knew how conservative and persecutory Pakistan is towards gay men, which is why he had to live in secret. During that period, the Appellant undertook XXXX XXXX XXXX studies in the USA. He lived in the USA from XXXX XXXX, 2006 to XXXX XXXX, 2008. He travelled back to Pakistan for two weeks in 2008 and then returned to live in the USA from 2008 to XXXX XXXX, 2010.

[27] The Appellant wrote that after the discovery of his relationship with Z. in XXXX 2011, the Appellant was forced to immediately move into a guesthouse and then flee Pakistan on the first available flight to the USA.12 The Appellant resumed his XXXX XXXX XXXX studies in the USA, which were already in progress. The Appellant has explained that he did not apply for asylum in the USA at this time because "I could not imagine leaving my studies, as obtaining a XXXX education had been my lifelong goal. I thus did not want to seek asylum in the USA..."13

[28] According to the Appellant, he completed his XXXX studies in 2012. He did not apply for asylum in the USA at this time, despite the fact that he had now completed his XXXX education, which was his stated goal above and the reason he had not applied earlier. Instead, the Appellant enrolled in a XXXX-XXXX XXXX program in 2013.

[29] The Appellant's registration in his XXXX-XXXX XXXX was terminated at the end of 2013. The Appellant's legal status in the USA was terminated around the same time. At this point, the Appellant wrote, he contacted attorneys to help him regularize his status (that allegation was found not to be credible in the section above). The attorneys allegedly told the Appellant that he had waited too long and he could no longer apply for asylum. There is no explanation why the Appellant did not pursue other avenues for regularization of his status in the USA at this time since his original stated goal was to finish his XXXX XXXX XXXX education (which he had now done) and apply for USA permanent residence on the basis of his education and work experience (which he had).

[30] In addition, the Appellant wrote that at this time he had not completely made up his mind about settling permanently in the West or thought of making an asylum claim in Canada because of his parents' plight in Pakistan (this allegation was also found not to be credible in the sections above).

[31] Instead of making attempts to regularize his status in the USA, the Appellant stayed in the USA illegally for approximately the next five years, from XXXX 2013 to XXXX 2018. The Appellant worked several jobs in the USA during this time. The Appellant wrote that in XXXX 2018, he researched how to get to Canada illegally and finally crossed to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018, where he made his refugee claim.

[32] The RPD found that, while the Appellant had attempted to portray himself as naïve when it comes to the refugee asylum process, he is actually quite sophisticated. The RPD noted that the Appellant is a XXXX XXXX, and that he had adduced an employment letter stating that he has "vast technical knowledge" and a "willingness to solve any issues at hand." The RPD found that the Appellant is XXXX savvy and resourceful, and that at any point during his stay in the USA he could have easily searched to find out about the USA asylum process. The RPD noted that the fear of returning to Pakistan allegedly crystalized in 2011, and found that the failure to claim status in the USA in the subsequent seven years undermined the credibility of his allegations. The RPD noted that failure to claim status in another country is relevant to subjective fear but is not in itself determinative or sufficient to rebut a presumption of truthfulness.

[33] The Appellant has argued on appeal that the RPD did treat the issue of failure to claim in the USA as determinative in its decision. The Appellant has argued that he provided a reasonable explanation for why he could not apply for asylum in the USA. He has argued that he did not apply because he was concerned he would be rejected, and has cited various country conditions showing that there is ongoing discrimination against Muslim people in the USA.

[34] In my independent review I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's failure to claim status in the USA is not reasonably explained and that this leads to a non-determinative negative credibility inference.

[35] The Appellant has mounted numerous separate explanations for his failure to claim at various times, none of which stand up to any scrutiny. The first explanation, that the Appellant did not want to apply for asylum in 2011 because he wanted to finish his XXXX XXXX XXXX degree in the USA, makes little sense to me because there would have been nothing stopping the Appellant from finishing his degree if he had applied for asylum at that time (there is no need to choose one or the other and the Appellant has not explained why he was under that impression). Further, when the Appellant did finish his XXXX XXXX XXXX degree he still did not make an attempt to apply for asylum or otherwise regularize his status. Instead, he worked and applied for further schooling.

[36] The Appellant's second explanation, that he contacted lawyers and was told he was now too late to apply for asylum was found not to be credible and I will not restate my reasons for this. Even if the Appellant did consult lawyers about asylum in around 2013, and was told he could not apply for asylum, this does not explain why he did not at this time pursue regularizing his status via other methods on the basis of his XXXX XXXX XXXX education and work experience, as was his stated earlier goal and the reason he did not apply for asylum within the legislated time period.

[37] The Appellant's third explanation, that he was concerned for his parents who were alone in Lahore with nobody to care for them and attempted to return twice to a highly persecutory situation to do so was also found not to be credible, and again I will not restate my reasons for this. Even if this was the case, it does not explain why the Appellant would have chosen to live and work illegally in the USA in a highly precarious situation with no status for five years instead of attempting to regularize his status.

[38] The Appellant's fourth explanation, that he did not apply for asylum in the USA because he was concerned that his claim would not be accepted and because of the ongoing discrimination against Muslim people in the USA is not sufficient in my opinion. While I accept that ongoing anti-Muslim discrimination in the USA is an objective concern, the Appellant made no mention of having this concern personally in his detailed narrative and explanations for his failure to claim. The explanation only arose at the RPD hearing. The facts of this case show that the Appellant was living, going to school, and working in the USA for a total of 12 years (from 2006 to 2018). The Appellant was not, so to speak, living under the radar in the USA during this time. He has alleged that apart from living, going to school, and working in the USA, he was actively socializing with other gay men and attending bars and nightclubs. I would expect that if anti-Muslim sentiment in the USA or fear of rejection were a significant factor in the Appellant's mind, the Appellant would have attempted to regularize his status elsewhere. I would also expect the Appellant to have at least articulated this reason in his narrative instead of including allegations about how active he was in USA society and how he planned to apply for status on the basis of his educational and work integration.

[39] I do not agree with the Appellant's assertion that the RPD treated this finding as determinative, because this finding is merely one of many that the RPD cited in its reasons for finding that the Appellant's presumption of truthfulness is rebutted. I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's failure to claim asylum in the USA over a 12 year period, but particularly in the seven-year period between 2011-2018, is not satisfactorily explained and that this failure warrants a non-determinative negative credibility inference.
No corroboration of personal relationships with other gay men

[40] The RPD noted that the Appellant alleged that he had been an active member of the gay community in the USA for at least five years, and that he had alleged that he was an active member of the Canadian gay community for approximately two years at the time of the RPD hearing. The Appellant wrote and testified that in this period, he had been going to bars and nightclubs, meeting numerous other gay people, and had engaged in numerous interpersonal relationships with other gay men, including sexual relationships. However, the Appellant testified that none of these relationships were long-lasting. The RPD noted that, before these relationships, the Appellant had alleged that he had an 11-year romantic relationship with Z., numerous years of which the relationship was maintained over long distance between the USA and Pakistan.

[41] The RPD noted that the Appellant had provided no corroborative evidence, such as photos or letters, from any other person with whom he had a personal connection in the gay community. The RPD noted that the Appellant had attended the 519 Community Centre in Toronto on a weekly basis from XXXX 2018 to XXXX 2020, and that he had allegedly been open about his orientation while there. The RPD found the lack of evidence from individuals in the gay community problematic, given the Appellant's specific allegations.

[42] The Appellant explained that he was too fearful to get evidence of his connections to other gay people but did not elaborate. He explained that he had never thought of getting a letter from anyone he met in Canada that had personal knowledge of his orientation.

[43] The RPD found that the lack of evidence was unreasonable for a bright, sophisticated XXXX graduate of the Appellant's profile. The RPD found that given the understandable lack of evidence from Pakistan, the Appellant would have been expected to have produced some sort of corroborative evidence of his allegedly extensive integration into the gay communities in the USA and Canada. The RPD noted that there are some instances in which it is not reasonable to expect evidence will be available, but no reason was given regarding why the Appellant could produce no evidence of his allegedly extensive public socializing in the USA.

[44] On appeal, the Appellant has argued that his relationship with Z. was secretive, and they lost contact after 2011, so it is unduly onerous to expect any evidence of that relationship. He has further argued that the expectation of evidence from the USA or Canada is unreasonable because he holds reasonable ongoing fears and reservations about his orientation, notwithstanding the fact that he has had numerous interpersonal relationships and has gone to bars and nightclubs in the USA. The Appellant has argued that the statement of attendance from the 519 Community Centre is corroborative evidence of his orientation and that the RPD ignored this. In any event, the Appellant argues, the lack of evidence finding is not based on inconsistencies and a lack of evidence is not sufficient on its own to rebut his presumption of truthfulness.

[45] In my independent assessment, I do consider it quite unusual that the Appellant in his personal circumstances is entirely unable to provide corroborative evidence from even one single personal connection. The Appellant was allegedly in a long-distance relationship for over 10 years, and though I understand that the relationship was secretive, the Appellant has made reference to both telephone communication and social media activity with Z. I find it quite unusual that the Appellant would be able to point to no "digital fingerprint" of the Appellant's past communications with Z. I find it more unusual that the Appellant is unable to provide evidence from any of his past personal connections in the gay communities in the USA and Canada. I do not accept the Appellant's explanation that he holds ongoing fears and reservations about his orientation in the USA and Canada. In my opinion, the Appellant's alleged public activities in which he has stated that he voluntarily attended numerous bars and nightclubs and had numerous personal relationships with people outweighs the fear of his orientation that I can accept he may hold. Even more unusual, in my opinion, is the fact that the Appellant has shown no particular interest in gathering this evidence. I have no evidence showing that the Appellant has attempted to find or reach out to any of his current or past connections in the gay community with whom he has ever socialized. Furthermore, I have no evidence showing that the Appellant has attempted to contact any of the bars or nightclubs the Appellant allegedly used to frequent in order to gather evidence of his past attendance or connections.

[46] I am mindful of the basic legal premise that there is no fundamental requirement for corroborative evidence. For this reason, I find that the lack of corroborative evidence of any personal connections to people in the gay community does not warrant its own negative credibility inference. However, this lack of corroborative evidence does mean that the claim must instead be decided on the remaining evidence that the Appellant has provided.
Letter from the 519 Community Centre

[47] The RPD did not directly address the letter from the 519 Community Centre (a well-known institutional hub for the gay community in Toronto). This was an error. The letter from the 519 states that the Appellant has attended a newcomer orientation session and that he has attended 13 weeks of an integration support group aimed at the 2SLGBT+ community. I consider this letter credible in confirming that the Appellant has, since he applied for refugee status in Canada, attended these sessions. The letter gives no indication that its author has any specific knowledge of the Appellant's other allegations or of his sexual orientation. However, I accept that the letter is supportive of the Appellant's allegations and it should be weighed against the credibility problems in the final credibility assessment.
Letter from the Appellant's father

[48] The RPD found that the letter from the Appellant's father was not credible, because the letter from the father omitted the allegation that the parents had to flee their hometown for Lahore as a result of the discovery of the Appellant's orientation in 2011. The RPD found that it was not credible that the father would omit this or forget this in his letter because it would have been traumatizing.

[49] On appeal, the Appellant has argued that this document is in fact an affidavit, not a letter. The Appellant argues that it is erroneous to judge it on what it does not say and that the letter is otherwise consistent with the Appellant's narrative.

[50] In my independent review, I do note that the letter contains some minor irregularities. First, the letter is not an affidavit as the Appellant has asserted. It is not sworn or notarized. It appears to me to simply be a letter that was typed, for a reason not explained, on Pakistani affidavit stamp paper. The letter itself uses several specific turns of phrase that are identical to those used in the Appellant's memorandum, which I find unusual since the two documents were allegedly written by different people. I take no negative inferences from these minor irregularities. The Federal Court has been clear that letters should be weighed for what they do say and not what they do not say. I find the RPD's approach to the letter to be erroneous and I take no negative credibility inference. I weigh the letter against the other evidence and the credibility problems above in my conclusion on credibility.
Medical letter

[51] The RPD found that the medical letter was dated XXXX XXXX, 2018 but referenced injuries from an assault that took place on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. The RPD noted that the report did not note the reason for the assault and that it therefore had limited probative value.
[52] The Appellant has argued that the report is consistent with his allegations and that the RPD erred by relying on what the report does not say rather than what it does say.

[53] In my independent review, I note that it is rather unusual that the clinic would write a letter in 2018 referencing a medical record from 2011 rather than simply providing the complete medical record from 2011 directly. In any event, the letter states that the Appellant presented with numerous minor injuries such as swelling, bruises and cuts following an assault.

[54] The medical letter causes no new credibility problems on its own and it deserves to be weighed against the credibility problems and other evidence in my final credibility determination.
Photo of two young men

[55] The Appellant adduced a photo of two young men that he stated was a photo of himself and Z. The RPD noted that the photo did not hint at romance and was simply a photo of two young men sitting in school desks one row apart. The RPD gave this photo no probative value.
[56] The Appellant has argued that it is unreasonable to give this photo no probative value given the secretive nature of his relationship with Z.

[57] In my independent review, I note that the photo causes no credibility problems of its own and it deserves to be weighed in the final credibility determination. I agree with the RPD that this photo is not probative of a romantic relationship, since it is not capable of proving that fact on its own.
Implausibility finding is erroneous

[58] The Appellant testified that he first realized he was attracted to other males around the age of 12 or 13. He testified that he was attracted to every boy in his class at that age, including the boys that were not physically attractive. Both the RPD member and the Appellant's counsel seemed surprised by this assertion, and the Appellant's counsel asked the Appellant to clarify. The Appellant again stated that he was attracted to every boy regardless of appearance.

[59] The RPD found that it was implausible that the Appellant would be attracted to every single boy, "even the ugly ones." The Appellant has argued on appeal that the RPD's finding is purely speculative and that there is nothing inherently unworthy of belief in the testimony.

[60] I am mindful of the Federal Court's guidance on implausibility findings, which states that they must only be made in the clearest of cases such as when the documentary evidence demonstrates that events could not have occurred in the manner described. In my opinion, though I may agree with the RPD that the Appellant's testimony on this issue seems unusual, this is not a clear case of implausibility and the RPD relied only on its own speculation in making this finding. I find this to have been erroneous and I take no negative inference from this testimony.
Conclusion on credibility: the Appellant's presumption of truthfulness is rebutted

[61] When I consider all the evidence as a whole, I find that I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted. I find this way because the Appellant has not reasonably explained various problems covering numerous areas of his core allegations of subjective fear, including his attempts to return to Pakistan, inconsistencies in his evidence related to his interactions with refugee lawyers, and his long-standing failure to claim status in the USA. The Appellant provided some corroborative documents, which I have considered, but I find that they collectively do not overcome or outweigh the credibility problems. I accept that the Appellant has attended a 2SLGBT+ meeting group since he initiated his refugee claim in Canada, but I find this insufficient to reliably establish his core allegation that he is a gay man given the other problems on the record. The Appellant showed no effort to gather other corroborative evidence of his past alleged personal relationships with other gay men, which may very well have overcome the credibility problems had it been reliably adduced. Due to the inconsistencies and other problems in the record, I find the Appellant's testimony and evidence unreliable on the core allegation that he is a gay man, that he has ever been suspected of being a gay man, that he has been persecuted in the past, and that he would face a serious possibility of persecution in the future. This finding is determinative of this appeal.
CONCLUSION

[62] The RPD made some credibility findings that I have determined are in error, but these errors were not fatal to its overall correct conclusion that the Appellant lacks credibility with respect to his allegations of his sexual orientation, his past persecution, and his forward-facing risk of persecution.

[63] The Appellant has not shown that he faces a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk to life, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture should he return to Pakistan.

[64] The Appellant is not a Convention refugee and is not a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed pursuant to IRPA s. 111(1)(a).
